claim: Apoptotic caspases have long been regarded as tumor suppressors.
source: Apoptosis and its molecular mediators, the caspases, have long been regarded as tumor suppressors and one hallmark of cancer is 'Evading Apoptosis'.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: One hallmark of cancer is 'Evading Apoptosis'.
source: Apoptosis and its molecular mediators, the caspases, have long been regarded as tumor suppressors and one hallmark of cancer is 'Evading Apoptosis'.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Recent work has suggested that apoptotic caspases can also promote proliferation and tumor growth under certain conditions.
source: However, recent work has suggested that apoptotic caspases can also promote proliferation and tumor growth under certain conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to other work mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Oncogenic mutations of the proto-oncogene Ras (RasV12) maintain tumorous cells in an 'undead'-like condition.
source: Here, we show that although caspases are activated in a well-studied neoplastic tumor model in Drosophila, oncogenic mutations of the proto-oncogene Ras (RasV12) maintain tumorous cells in an 'undead'-like condition and transform caspases from tumor suppressors into tumor promotors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: RasV12 transforms caspases from tumor suppressors into tumor promotors.
source: Here, we show that although caspases are activated in a well-studied neoplastic tumor model in Drosophila, oncogenic mutations of the proto-oncogene Ras (RasV12) maintain tumorous cells in an 'undead'-like condition and transform caspases from tumor suppressors into tumor promotors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Caspases promote the generation of intra- and extracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
source: Instead of killing cells, caspases now promote the generation of intra- and extracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: ROS recruit and activate macrophage-like immune cells (hemocytes).
source: One function of the ROS is the recruitment and activation of macrophage-like immune cells which in turn signal back to tumorous epithelial cells to activate oncogenic JNK signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Hemocytes signal back to tumorous epithelial cells to activate oncogenic JNK signaling.
source: One function of the ROS is the recruitment and activation of macrophage-like immune cells which in turn signal back to tumorous epithelial cells to activate oncogenic JNK signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: JNK further promotes and amplifies caspase activity, thereby constituting a feedback amplification loop.
source: JNK further promotes and amplifies caspase activity, thereby constituting a feedback amplification loop.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Interfering with the amplification loop strongly reduces the neoplastic behavior of scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
source: Interfering with the amplification loop strongly reduces the neoplastic behavior of these cells and significantly improves organismal survival.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Interfering with the amplification loop significantly improves organismal survival.
source: Interfering with the amplification loop strongly reduces the neoplastic behavior of these cells and significantly improves organismal survival.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Larval imaginal discs in Drosophila are single-cell layered sacs of epithelial cells that develop into the adult appendages such as eyes and wings.
source: Larval imaginal discs in Drosophila are single-cell layered sacs of epithelial cells that develop into the adult appendages such as eyes and wings, and are frequently used as genetic models for growth control and tumor development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Maintenance of apical-basal polarity of epithelial cells is critical for suppression of neoplastic tumor development.
source: Maintenance of apical-basal polarity of epithelial cells is critical for suppression of neoplastic tumor development (Elsum et al., 2012; Bergstralh and St Johnston, 2012; Martin-Belmonte and Perez-Moreno, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding components of the Scribble complex including scribble (scrib), lethal giant larvae (lgl) and discs large (dlg) disrupt apical-basal polarity in epithelial cells which can trigger malignant neoplastic tumor growth.
source: Mutations in genes encoding components of the Scribble complex including scribble (scrib), lethal giant larvae (lgl) and discs large (dlg) disrupt apical-basal polarity in epithelial cells which can trigger malignant neoplastic tumor growth (Bergstralh and St Johnston, 2012; Elsum et al., 2012; Bilder et al., 2000; Gateff, 1978; Bilder and Perrimon, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Drosophila larvae entirely mutant for scrib fail to respond to stop signals of growth, fail to pupariate and continue to grow as larvae.
source: Drosophila larvae entirely mutant for scrib fail to respond to stop signals of growth, fail to pupariate and continue to grow as larvae (Gateff, 1994; Wodarz, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Drosophila larvae entirely mutant for scrib die as giant larvae with severely overgrown imaginal discs.
source: They die as giant larvae with severely overgrown imaginal discs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: scrib mutant cells (clones) in otherwise wild-type imaginal discs are eliminated by cell competition mediated by neighboring wild-type cells.
source: However, scrib mutant cells (clones) in otherwise wild-type imaginal discs are eliminated by cell competition mediated by neighboring wild-type cells (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Menéndez et al., 2010; Igaki et al., 2009; Uhlirova et al., 2005; Ohsawa et al., 2011; Leong et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2012; Vaughen and Igaki, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Eiger, the Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha (TNFα)-like ligand in Drosophila, triggers Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) activation and apoptosis in scrib mutant cells in response to cell competition.
source: Mechanistically, in response to cell competition, Eiger, the Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha (TNFα)-like ligand in Drosophila, triggers Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) activation and apoptosis in scrib mutant cells (Igaki et al., 2009; Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Uhlirova et al., 2005; Cordero et al., 2010; Ohsawa et al., 2011; Leong et al., 2009; Igaki et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The tumor-suppressing function of Eiger and JNK in scrib mutant cells is dependent on induction of apoptosis.
source: This tumor-suppressing function is dependent on Eiger and JNK through induction of apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of Eiger or JNK restores the growth potential of scrib mutant cells which can then form large tumor masses in imaginal discs.
source: Inhibition of Eiger or JNK restores the growth potential of scrib mutant cells which can then form large tumor masses in imaginal discs (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2009; Uhlirova et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: scrib−/− RasV12 cells can unleash their full malignant potential when additional oncogenic mutations such as RasV12 are introduced into scrib mutant cells.
source: However, if additional oncogenic mutations such as RasV12 are introduced into scrib mutant cells (referred to a scrib−/− RasV12), they can unleash their full malignant potential (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Pagliarini and Xu, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic eye/antennal imaginal discs display all neoplastic features observed in human tumors including unrestricted growth, failure to differentiate, tissue invasion and organismal lethality.
source: scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic eye/antennal imaginal discs display all neoplastic features observed in human tumors including unrestricted growth, failure to differentiate, tissue invasion and organismal lethality (Pagliarini and Xu, 2003; Brumby and Richardson, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: scrib−/− RasV12 clones occupy a large portion of the mosaic disc and trigger multi-layered overgrowth of the entire disc compared to wild-type controls.
source: scrib−/− RasV12 clones occupy a large portion of the mosaic disc and trigger multi-layered overgrowth of the entire disc compared to wild-type controls (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H,I.

claim: scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells invade other tissues, most notably the ventral nerve cord (VNC) in the brain.
source: scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells also invade other tissues, most notably the ventral nerve cord (VNC) in the brain (Figure 1H,I) (Pagliarini and Xu, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H,I and citations to previous work.

claim: The scrib−/− RasV12 condition in ey-FLP-induced eye imaginal disc mosaics is 100% lethal.
source: The scrib−/− RasV12 condition in ey-FLP-induced eye imaginal disc mosaics is 100% lethal.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: 95% of ey-FLP-induced scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals die as larvae.
source: 95% of ey-FLP-induced scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals die as larvae; the remaining animals die during pupal stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The remaining 5% of ey-FLP-induced scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals die during pupal stages.
source: 95% of ey-FLP-induced scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals die as larvae; the remaining animals die during pupal stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: RasV12 inhibits the apoptotic activity of JNK and converts the tumor-suppressor function of Eiger and JNK in scrib−/− cells into a tumor-promoting one in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
source: Interestingly, RasV12 inhibits the apoptotic activity of JNK and converts the tumor-suppressor function of Eiger and JNK in scrib−/− cells into a tumor-promoting one in scrib−/− RasV12 cells (Enomoto et al., 2015; Cordero et al., 2010; Uhlirova et al., 2005; Igaki et al., 2006; Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The aggressive tumor growth of scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones becomes dependent on Eiger and JNK.
source: Therefore, the aggressive tumor growth of scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones becomes dependent on Eiger and JNK (Igaki et al., 2006; Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006; Brumby et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It is not understood how RasV12 promotes the oncogenic switch of Eiger and JNK.
source: Mechanistically, it is not understood how RasV12 promotes this oncogenic switch of Eiger and JNK.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Caspases are Cys-proteases that mediate the mechanistic events of apoptotic cell death.
source: Caspases are Cys-proteases that mediate the mechanistic events of apoptotic cell death (Shalini et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2009; Fuchs and Steller, 2011; Salvesen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Caspases are synthesized as zymogens and depending on the length of their prodomains can be classified into initiator and effector caspases.
source: They are synthesized as zymogens and depending on the length of their prodomains can be classified into initiator and effector caspases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about caspases.

claim: Initiator caspases such as mammalian Caspase-9 or its Drosophila ortholog Dronc are controlled by upstream signaling events and when activated initiate apoptosis by activating effector caspases.
source: Initiator caspases such as mammalian Caspase-9 or its Drosophila ortholog Dronc are controlled by upstream signaling events and when activated initiate apoptosis by activating effector caspases such as mammalian Caspase-3 or its Drosophila ortholog DrICE (Fuchs and Steller, 2011; Shalini et al., 2015; Salvesen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Caspases induce apoptosis of many cells to maintain homeostatic conditions, and are also thought to be critical for tumor suppression by eliminating malignant cells.
source: Caspases induce apoptosis of many cells to maintain homeostatic conditions, and are also thought to be critical for tumor suppression by eliminating malignant cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about caspases.

claim: Caspases can have tumor-promoting roles, for example through apoptosis-induced proliferation (AiP).
source: However, caspases can also have tumor-promoting roles, for example through apoptosis-induced proliferation (AiP), a caspase-driven process by which apoptotic cells produce mitogenic signals for proliferation of neighboring surviving cells (Mollereau et al., 2013) (reviewed in [Fogarty and Bergmann, 2017; Ryoo and Bergmann, 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Apoptosis-induced proliferation (AiP) is a caspase-driven process by which apoptotic cells produce mitogenic signals for proliferation of neighboring surviving cells.
source: However, caspases can also have tumor-promoting roles, for example through apoptosis-induced proliferation (AiP), a caspase-driven process by which apoptotic cells produce mitogenic signals for proliferation of neighboring surviving cells (Mollereau et al., 2013) (reviewed in [Fogarty and Bergmann, 2017; Ryoo and Bergmann, 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There are two types of AiP: 'genuine' AiP and 'undead' AiP.
source: There are two types of AiP. During 'genuine' AiP, apoptotic cells release mitogenic factors before completing the apoptotic program. This type of AiP has been described for regeneration and wound healing both in vertebrates and invertebrates (Tseng et al., 2007; Fan and Bergmann, 2008; Chera et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010). 'Genuine' AiP may also be involved in human pathologies such as cancer, and may account for increased cell proliferation and repopulation of tumors following cytotoxic treatments (chemo- or radiotherapy) which induces massive apoptosis (reviewed in [Fogarty and Bergmann, 2017; Ichim and Tait, 2016]). Caspases play significant tumor-promoting roles in these settings (Li et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2011; Donato et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Kurtova et al., 2015). The second type is 'undead' AiP.
evidence: This is inferred from the description of two distinct types of AiP in the text.

claim: During 'genuine' AiP, apoptotic cells release mitogenic factors before completing the apoptotic program.
source: During 'genuine' AiP, apoptotic cells release mitogenic factors before completing the apoptotic program.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 'Genuine' AiP has been described for regeneration and wound healing both in vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: This type of AiP has been described for regeneration and wound healing both in vertebrates and invertebrates (Tseng et al., 2007; Fan and Bergmann, 2008; Chera et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 'Genuine' AiP may be involved in human pathologies such as cancer, and may account for increased cell proliferation and repopulation of tumors following cytotoxic treatments.
source: 'Genuine' AiP may also be involved in human pathologies such as cancer, and may account for increased cell proliferation and repopulation of tumors following cytotoxic treatments (chemo- or radiotherapy) which induces massive apoptosis (reviewed in [Fogarty and Bergmann, 2017; Ichim and Tait, 2016]).
evidence: This is speculative and supported by citations to reviews.

claim: Caspases play significant tumor-promoting roles in 'genuine' AiP settings.
source: Caspases play significant tumor-promoting roles in these settings (Li et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2011; Donato et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Kurtova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In 'undead' AiP, the apoptosis pathway is induced upstream, but the execution of apoptosis is blocked.
source: The second type is 'undead' AiP. Here, the apoptosis pathway is induced upstream, but the execution of apoptosis is blocked.
evidence: This is a description of the 'undead' AiP model.

claim: In Drosophila, apoptosis inhibition in 'undead' AiP is achieved experimentally by expression of the effector caspase inhibitor p35 which very specifically inhibits DrICE.
source: In Drosophila, apoptosis inhibition is achieved experimentally by expression of the effector caspase inhibitor p35 which very specifically inhibits DrICE (Hay et al., 1994; Meier et al., 2000; Hawkins et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In 'undead' cells, non-apoptotic functions of active Dronc can be examined, one of which is the release of mitogenic signals for induction of AiP which can lead to hyperplastic overgrowth.
source: In 'undead' cells, non-apoptotic functions of active Dronc can now be examined, one of which is the release of mitogenic signals for induction of AiP which can lead to hyperplastic overgrowth (Wells et al., 2006; Kondo et al., 2006; Huh et al., 2004; Ryoo et al., 2004; Martín et al., 2009; Pérez-Garijo et al., 2009; Pérez-Garijo et al., 2004; Fan et al., 2014; Rudrapatna et al., 2013; Pérez-Garijo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 'Undead' states of cells may be present under pathological conditions.
source: 'Undead' states of cells may also be present under pathological conditions.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: It has been proposed that RasV12 can maintain apoptotic cells in an 'undead'-like state promoting tumorigenesis.
source: For instance, it has been proposed that RasV12 can maintain apoptotic cells in an 'undead'-like state promoting tumorigenesis (Hirabayashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: AiP-mediated hyperplastic overgrowth of 'undead' tissue depends on a Dronc-initiated feedback amplification loop which involves reactive oxygen species (ROS), activation of macrophage-like hemocytes, secretion of Eiger by hemocytes, Eiger-dependent activation of JNK in epithelial disc and further activation of Dronc by JNK.
source: Mechanistically, we have shown that AiP-mediated hyperplastic overgrowth of 'undead' tissue depends on a Dronc-initiated feedback amplification loop which involves reactive oxygen species (ROS) – specifically extracellular ROS produced by the membrane-bound NADPH oxidase Duox –, activation of macrophage-like hemocytes, secretion of Eiger by hemocytes, Eiger-dependent activation of JNK in epithelial disc and further activation of Dronc by JNK (Fogarty et al., 2016) (reviewed by [Diwanji and Bergmann, 2017a; Diwanji and Bergmann, 2017b]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Extracellular ROS in 'undead' AiP are produced by the membrane-bound NADPH oxidase Duox.
source: Mechanistically, we have shown that AiP-mediated hyperplastic overgrowth of 'undead' tissue depends on a Dronc-initiated feedback amplification loop which involves reactive oxygen species (ROS) – specifically extracellular ROS produced by the membrane-bound NADPH oxidase Duox –, activation of macrophage-like hemocytes, secretion of Eiger by hemocytes, Eiger-dependent activation of JNK in epithelial disc and further activation of Dronc by JNK (Fogarty et al., 2016) (reviewed by [Diwanji and Bergmann, 2017a; Diwanji and Bergmann, 2017b]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Eiger and JNK signaling have proliferation- and growth-promoting functions in the 'undead' AiP model.
source: Therefore, similar to the scrib−/− RasV12 case, Eiger and JNK signaling have proliferation- and growth-promoting functions in this 'undead' AiP model.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: ROS levels are significantly higher in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones compared to wt (FRT +), scrib−/− or RasV12-expressing clones.
source: (F) DHE quantification reveals that ROS levels are significantly higher in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones compared to wt (FRT +), scrib−/− or RasV12-expressing clones.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Reduction of extra- and intracellular ROS levels in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones significantly improves the pupariation rates of animals bearing scrib RasV12 mosaic eye imaginal discs.
source: (G) Reduction of extra- and intracellular ROS levels in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones significantly improves the pupariation rates of animals bearing scrib RasV12 mosaic eye imaginal discs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Expression of UAS-lacZ in scrib−/− RasV12 clones as control has no effect on the pupariation rate.
source: Expression of UAS-lacZ in scrib−/− RasV12 clones as control has no effect on the pupariation rate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Depletion of ROS strongly reduces clone size and normalizes growth in scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs.
source: (H–N) Cephalic complexes composed of eye/antennal discs, optic lobes (OL) and ventral nerve cord (VNC) from day 11 old third instar larvae. The genotype is indicated on top of each panel. Expression of UAS-lacZ served as negative control (I). Depletion of ROS strongly reduces clone size (green) and normalizes growth in (J–N).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H-N.

claim: ey-FLP-induced scrib−/− RasV12 MARCM mosaics are 100% lethal (0% adult survival).
source: Note that ey-FLP-induced scrib−/− RasV12 MARCM mosaics are 100% lethal (0% adult survival) (P).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: Expression of antioxidant transgenes in scrib−/− RasV12 clones allows some adult survival.
source: (O–U) Adult eyes of control (O) and scrib−/− RasV12 mosaics expressing the indicated antioxidant transgenes (Q–U). The percentage number in the top right of each panel indicates the adult survival rate relative to pupal survival.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1O-U.

claim: There is strong increase of H2DCF-CA labeling in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones in a caspase-dependent manner.
source: There is strong increase of H2DCF-CA labeling in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones in a caspase-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ROS levels are significantly higher in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones compared to wt (FRT +) and RasV12 clones as measured by H2DCF-CA.
source: (G) Quantification of H2DCF-CA labelings revealed that ROS levels are significantly higher in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones (C) compared to wt (FRT +) (A) and RasV12 (B) clones.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Loss of caspase activity significantly reduces H2DCF-CA labelings in scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
source: Loss of caspase activity also significantly reduces H2DCF-CA labelings (D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Removing extracellular ROS by UAS-Duox RNAi or overexpression of the UAS-hCatS transgene strongly suppressed tumor growth of scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells.
source: In contrast, removing extracellular ROS by UAS-Duox RNAi or overexpression of the UAS-hCatS transgene which encodes a secreted human catalase (Ha et al., 2005b2005; Ha et al., 2005a), strongly suppressed tumor growth of scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells (Figure 1J,K) suggesting that extracellular ROS are required for tumor growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J,K.

claim: Extracellular ROS are required for tumor growth of scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
source: In contrast, removing extracellular ROS by UAS-Duox RNAi or overexpression of the UAS-hCatS transgene which encodes a secreted human catalase (Ha et al., 2005b2005; Ha et al., 2005a), strongly suppressed tumor growth of scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells (Figure 1J,K) suggesting that extracellular ROS are required for tumor growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the suppression of tumor growth upon removal of extracellular ROS.

claim: Removing intracellular ROS by misexpression of intracellular Catalase, SOD1 and SOD2 strongly suppressed tumor growth of scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
source: Interestingly and in contrast to the 'undead' AiP model, removing intracellular ROS by misexpression of intracellular Catalase, SOD1 and SOD2 also strongly suppressed tumor growth (Figure 1L–N).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L-N.

claim: Both intra- and extracellular ROS are required for tumor growth of scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
source: These results suggest that both intra- and extracellular ROS are required for tumor growth of scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
evidence: This is inferred from the suppression of tumor growth upon removal of either intracellular or extracellular ROS.

claim: Reduction of ROS strongly reduces the invasive behavior of scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells.
source: Importantly also, reduction of ROS strongly reduces the invasive behavior of scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells (Figure 1J–N) which significantly improves the survival rate of the affected animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J-N.

claim: Reduction of ROS significantly improves the survival rate of scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals.
source: Importantly also, reduction of ROS strongly reduces the invasive behavior of scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells (Figure 1J–N) which significantly improves the survival rate of the affected animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J-N.

claim: Between 40% and 70% of the ey >MARCM scrib−/− RasV12 larvae expressing antioxidant enzymes develop into pupae compared to 5% for scrib−/− RasV12 only.
source: Compared to ey >MARCM scrib−/− RasV12 mutant larvae, of which only 5% reach pupal stages, between 40% and 70% of the ey >MARCM scrib−/− RasV12 larvae expressing antioxidant enzymes develop into pupae (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Viable adult ey >MARCM scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals expressing antioxidant genes were recovered at a low rate (5–15% of the surviving pupae).
source: Furthermore, we also recovered viable adult ey >MARCM scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals expressing antioxidant genes, although at a low rate (5–15% of the surviving pupae), which was never observed for scrib−/− RasV12 only (Figure 1P–U).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1P-U.

claim: Viable adult ey >MARCM scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals expressing antioxidant genes have deformed and weakly overgrown eyes and heads often with necrotic patches compared to wt control.
source: Although their eyes and heads are deformed and weakly overgrown often with necrotic patches compared to wt control (Figure 1O,Q–U), these animals live!
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1O,Q-U.

claim: Previously, only few examples of surviving scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals have been reported.
source: Previously, only few examples of surviving scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals have been reported.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Viable scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals were recovered when essential steps in tumor development such as oncogenic JNK signaling or the cell cycle were inhibited in scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
source: In these examples, viable scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals were recovered when essential steps in tumor development such as oncogenic JNK signaling or the cell cycle were inhibited in scrib−/− RasV12 clones (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Külshammer et al., 2015; Külshammer and Uhlirova, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The observation that reduction of ROS suppresses tumor growth and enhances organismal survival strongly suggests that ROS play a very significant role for the neoplastic characteristics of scrib−/− RasV12 animals.
source: Therefore, the observation that reduction of ROS suppresses tumor growth and enhances organismal survival strongly suggests that ROS play a very significant role for the neoplastic characteristics of scrib−/− RasV12 animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing suppression of tumor growth and improved survival upon ROS reduction.

claim: The initiator caspase Dronc (caspase-9 ortholog) has been shown to stimulate the production of ROS in 'undead' cells.
source: In 'undead' cells, the initiator caspase Dronc (caspase-9 ortholog) has been shown to stimulate the production of ROS (Fogarty et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Removing or inhibiting caspases in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones strongly reduced DHE labeling suggesting suppression of ROS generation.
source: Removing or inhibiting caspases in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones strongly reduced DHE labeling suggesting suppression of ROS generation (Figure 2A–D'; quantified in Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: Tumor overgrowth and invasion of the VNC is dramatically reduced upon removal or inhibition of caspases in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells.
source: Consequently, tumor overgrowth and invasion of the VNC is dramatically reduced upon removal or inhibition of caspases in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: Reduction of caspase activity increases pupal survival of scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals.
source: Reduction of caspase activity also increases pupal survival (Figure 2N) and viable animals with mosaic scrib−/− RasV12 heads and eyes were recovered as adults at a rate of 4–9% of the surviving pupae (Figure 2J–M).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2N.

claim: Viable animals with mosaic scrib−/− RasV12 heads and eyes were recovered as adults at a rate of 4–9% of the surviving pupae when caspase activity was reduced.
source: Reduction of caspase activity also increases pupal survival (Figure 2N) and viable animals with mosaic scrib−/− RasV12 heads and eyes were recovered as adults at a rate of 4–9% of the surviving pupae (Figure 2J–M).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J-M.

claim: The requirement of caspases for generation of ROS and neoplastic behavior suggests that caspases are activated in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells.
source: The requirement of caspases for generation of ROS and neoplastic behavior suggests that caspases are activated in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that caspases are required for ROS generation and tumor growth.

claim: scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones label significantly stronger with CC3 antibody compared to mosaic control discs (FRT +).
source: Indeed, while there is very little CC3 labeling in mosaic control discs (FRT +), scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones label significantly stronger with CC3 antibody (Figure 3A–B', yellow arrowhead; quantified in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: There is CC3 staining immediately outside scrib−/− RasV12 clones which appears even more intense than the labeling inside the clones.
source: In addition to the CC3 labeling in scrib−/− RasV12 clones, there is also staining immediately outside the clones which appears even more intense than the labeling inside the clones (Figure 3B,B'; white arrows).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,B'.

claim: Non-autonomous CC3 labeling outside scrib−/− RasV12 clones is 2 to 2.5-fold higher than autonomous CC3 labeling inside scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
source: In fact, quantification reveals that this non-autonomous CC3 labeling is 2 to 2.5-fold higher than autonomous CC3 labeling in scrib−/− RasV12 clones (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both CC3 labeling inside and outside of scrib−/− RasV12 clones are autonomously dependent on the caspases DrICE and Dronc as well as on ROS.
source: Both, CC3 labeling inside and outside of scrib−/− RasV12 clones are autonomously dependent on the caspases DrICE (Figure 3C) and Dronc as well as on ROS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A few TUNEL-positive cells are detectable within scrib−/− RasV12 clones, but the majority of TUNEL-positive cells are located outside the clones.
source: Interestingly, although a few TUNEL-positive cells are detectable within scrib−/− RasV12 clones, the majority of TUNEL-positive cells are located outside the clones (Figure 3E,E'; arrows).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,E'.

claim: Almost 90% of all apoptotic cells in scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs are outside of mutant clones.
source: Quantification reveals that almost 90% of all apoptotic cells in scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs are outside the mutant clones (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Despite detectable caspase (Dronc) activity in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones by CC3 labeling, this activity does not appear to trigger a significant amount of apoptosis in these clones.
source: Despite detectable caspase (Dronc) activity in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones by CC3 labeling, this activity does not appear to trigger a significant amount of apoptosis in these clones.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most TUNEL-positive cells are outside the clones despite CC3 labeling inside the clones.

claim: The strong tumor growth phenotype of scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic eye discs is dependent on caspases.
source: In contrast, our genetic analysis suggest that the strong tumor growth phenotype of scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic eye discs is dependent on caspases (Figure 2) suggesting that they have adopted a tumor-promoting function.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Caspases in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells have adopted a tumor-promoting function.
source: In contrast, our genetic analysis suggest that the strong tumor growth phenotype of scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic eye discs is dependent on caspases (Figure 2) suggesting that they have adopted a tumor-promoting function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tumor growth depends on caspases but caspases do not induce significant apoptosis in the tumor cells.

claim: Caspase activity in scrib−/− single mutant cells acts as a tumor suppressor by killing them.
source: In fact, caspase activity in scrib−/− single mutant cells does act as a tumor suppressor by killing them (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2006; Igaki et al., 2009; Uhlirova et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells, caspase activity persists, but does not appear to induce a significant amount of apoptosis.
source: In contrast, in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells, this caspase activity persists, but does not appear to induce a significant amount of apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing CC3 labeling but few TUNEL-positive cells in scrib−/− RasV12 clones.

claim: RasV12 maintains scrib−/− cells in an 'undead'-like condition.
source: Therefore, these data suggest that RasV12 maintains scrib−/− cells in an 'undead'-like condition, consistent with a previous report (Hirabayashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RasV12 changes the activity of caspases to adopt a tumor-promoting role.
source: Furthermore, RasV12 changes the activity of caspases to adopt a tumor-promoting role.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that caspases promote tumor growth in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.

claim: One known function of extracellular ROS is the recruitment and activation of Drosophila macrophages (hemocytes) in the 'undead' AiP model.
source: One known function of extracellular ROS is the recruitment and activation of Drosophila macrophages (hemocytes) in the 'undead' AiP model (Diwanji and Bergmann, 2017a; Fogarty et al., 2016; Diwanji and Bergmann, 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Hemocytes have been shown to be associated with scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs.
source: Hemocytes have been shown to be associated with scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs (Cordero et al., 2010; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Külshammer and Uhlirova, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At control discs, hemocytes adhere in small cellular aggregates, mostly at the antennal disc.
source: At control discs, hemocytes adhere in small cellular aggregates, mostly at the antennal disc (Figure 4A,A',L).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,A',L.

claim: Hemocytes are recruited to neoplastic scrib−/− RasV12 tumor sites in large numbers where they cover the eye portion of the disc.
source: In contrast, they are recruited to neoplastic scrib−/− RasV12 tumor sites in large numbers where they cover the eye portion of the disc (Figure 4B,B'; quantified in Figure 4K) consistent with previous reports (Cordero et al., 2010; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Külshammer and Uhlirova, 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,B',K and citations to previous work.

claim: Hemocytes change their morphological appearance at neoplastic scrib−/− RasV12 discs by singling out from cellular clusters and developing cellular protrusions, similar to cytonemes.
source: They also change their morphological appearance at neoplastic scrib−/− RasV12 discs. They single out from the cellular clusters and develop cellular protrusions, similar to cytonemes (Figure 4M, arrows).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: This change in cellular behavior and morphology of hemocytes was also observed in the 'undead' AiP model.
source: This change in cellular behavior and morphology of hemocytes was also observed in the 'undead' AiP model (Fogarty et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Reduction of ROS strongly reduces the recruitment of hemocytes to scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs.
source: Indeed, reduction of ROS strongly reduces the recruitment of hemocytes to scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs (Figure 4C–F').
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-F'.

claim: The recruitment of hemocytes to scrib−/− RasV12 tumors is impaired by loss of caspase activity.
source: Likewise, the recruitment of hemocytes to scrib−/− RasV12 tumors is impaired by loss of caspase activity (Figure 4G–I').
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-I'.

claim: Quantification of hemocyte recruitment to ROS-depleted or caspase-inhibited scrib−/− RasV12 discs normalized to GFP revealed a significant loss of hemocytes compared to scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs.
source: Quantification of hemocyte recruitment to ROS-depleted or caspase-inhibited scrib−/− RasV12 discs normalized to GFP (to account for the reduced size of ROS-depleted or caspase-inhibited scrib−/− RasV12 clones), revealed a significant loss of hemocytes compared to scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: More than 90% of scrib−/− RasV12 discs expressing Duox RNAi are not attached by any hemocyte despite the presence of many small clones.
source: For example, more than 90% of scrib−/− RasV12 discs expressing Duox RNAi are not attached by any hemocyte despite the presence of many small clones (Figure 4C').
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C'.

claim: The few hemocytes that are attached to ROS- and caspase-depleted scrib RasV12 discs display the naive morphology seen at control discs.
source: Furthermore, in addition to the significant loss of hemocytes, the few hemocytes that are attached to ROS- and caspase-depleted scrib RasV12 discs (Figure 4D'–I'), display the naive morphology seen at control discs (Figure 4N–R).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D'-I' and Figure 4N-R.

claim: Caspase-dependent generation of ROS is essential for recruitment and activation of hemocytes to scrib−/− RasV12 tumors.
source: These observations provide strong evidence that caspase-dependent generation of ROS is essential for recruitment and activation of hemocytes to scrib−/− RasV12 tumors.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that both ROS and caspases are required for hemocyte recruitment and activation.

claim: JNK activity is strongly induced in scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
source: As reported previously, JNK activity is strongly induced in scrib−/− RasV12 clones (Figure 5C) and is essential for the neoplastic phenotype of scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2006; Igaki et al., 2009; Uhlirova et al., 2005; Leong et al., 2009; Cordero et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and citations to previous work.

claim: JNK activity is essential for the neoplastic phenotype of scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals.
source: As reported previously, JNK activity is strongly induced in scrib−/− RasV12 clones (Figure 5C) and is essential for the neoplastic phenotype of scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic animals (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2006; Igaki et al., 2009; Uhlirova et al., 2005; Leong et al., 2009; Cordero et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activation of JNK in oncogenic RasV12 background is sufficient to trigger a neoplastic tumor phenotype similar to the scrib−/− RasV12 condition.
source: In fact, activation of JNK in oncogenic RasV12 background is sufficient to trigger a neoplastic tumor phenotype similar to the scrib−/− RasV12 condition (Uhlirova et al., 2005; Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In JNKDN-expressing scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones, caspase activity (CC3) and ROS production are strongly reduced.
source: In JNKDN-expressing scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones, caspase activity (CC3) and ROS production are strongly reduced (Figure 5A–B').
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B'.

claim: The recruitment and activation of hemocytes is strongly impaired at JNKDN; scrib−/− RasV12 discs.
source: Likewise, the recruitment and activation of hemocytes is strongly impaired at JNKDN; scrib−/− RasV12 discs (Figure 4J) consistent with a previous report (Külshammer and Uhlirova, 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J and a citation to previous work.

claim: Caspase activation, ROS generation and hemocyte activation are dependent on JNK signaling.
source: These findings suggest that caspase activation, ROS generation and hemocyte activation are dependent on JNK signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that blocking JNK reduces caspase activity, ROS production, and hemocyte recruitment.

claim: The strong pJNK labeling in scrib−/− RasV12 clones is significantly reduced upon ROS-depletion or reduction of caspase activity.
source: (L) The mean intensity of pJNK labelings in scrib−/− RasV12 clones in panels (C'–K') is significantly reduced upon ROS-depletion or reduction of caspase activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: There is a significant loss of JNK activity in caspase-inhibited or ROS-depleted scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
source: These labelings revealed a significant loss of JNK activity in caspase-inhibited or ROS-depleted scrib−/− RasV12 clones (Figure 5D–K'; quantified in Figure 5L).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-L.

claim: The maintenance of JNK activity requires caspases and ROS.
source: These observations suggest that the maintenance of JNK activity requires caspases and ROS.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that JNK activity is reduced when caspases or ROS are depleted.

claim: JNK is acting both upstream and downstream of caspases and ROS.
source: Combined, these results imply that JNK is acting both upstream (Figure 5A,B) and downstream (Figure 5E–L) of caspases and ROS.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing mutual dependence between JNK, caspases, and ROS.

claim: Caspases, ROS, hemocytes and JNK signaling constitute an amplification loop in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones.
source: The easiest way to explain such a behavior is that caspases, ROS, hemocytes and JNK signaling constitute an amplification loop in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones similar to the 'undead' AiP model (Diwanji and Bergmann, 2017a; Fogarty et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutual dependence of JNK, caspases, ROS, and hemocytes.

claim: The traditional view of caspases holds that they counter tumorigenesis by eliminating tumor cells and thus mediate a tumor suppressor function.
source: The traditional view of caspases holds that they counter tumorigenesis by eliminating tumor cells and thus mediate a tumor suppressor function (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2000; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The tumor-suppressing function of caspases has been reported in mammalian systems and in Drosophila.
source: This tumor-suppressing function of caspases has been reported in mammalian systems (Asselin-Labat et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2009) and in Drosophila, where, for example, scrib mutant cells undergo caspase-dependent apoptosis in a JNK- and Eiger-dependent manner (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2006; Igaki et al., 2009; Uhlirova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: More recent work has suggested that caspases and apoptosis in general can also have the opposite, tumor-promoting function, both in flies and in mammals.
source: However, more recent work has suggested that caspases and apoptosis in general can also have the opposite, tumor-promoting function, both in flies and in mammals (Cheng et al., 2015; Donato et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2011; Kurtova et al., 2015; Li et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2015); reviewed by (Ryoo and Bergmann, 2012; Ichim and Tait, 2016; Fogarty and Bergmann, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Drosophila it was previously shown that oncogenic Ras switches the tumor-suppressing function of JNK and Eiger in scrib−/− mutant cells to a tumor-promoting one in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
source: Furthermore, in Drosophila it was previously shown that oncogenic Ras switches the tumor-suppressing function of JNK and Eiger in scrib−/− mutant cells to a tumor-promoting one in scrib−/− RasV12 cells (Igaki et al., 2006; Cordero et al., 2010; Uhlirova et al., 2005; Enomoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mechanistic details about the oncogenic switch of JNK and Eiger by RasV12 have been largely elusive.
source: Mechanistic details about this oncogenic switch have been largely elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: A critical step for the oncogenic switch of JNK and Eiger is the conversion of caspase activity by oncogenic Ras.
source: Our data presented here imply that a critical step for this oncogenic switch is the conversion of caspase activity by oncogenic Ras.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that caspases are required for tumor growth in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.

claim: Oncogenic Ras can suppress the apoptotic activity of caspases and keeps scrib−/− RasV12 cells in an 'undead'-like condition.
source: Consistent with a previous report in different context (Hirabayashi et al., 2013), our results demonstrated that oncogenic Ras can suppress the apoptotic activity of caspases and keeps scrib−/− RasV12 cells in an 'undead'-like condition.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and a citation to previous work.

claim: While caspases may still induce apoptosis in a few tumor cells, they now largely promote generation of intra- and extracellular ROS which are required for malignant growth and tissue invasion of surviving neoplastic cells.
source: While caspases may still induce apoptosis in a few tumor cells, they now largely promote generation of intra- and extracellular ROS which are required for malignant growth and tissue invasion of surviving neoplastic cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Evidence that caspases are indeed activated in scrib−/− RasV12 clones is provided in this study and in a report that showed that small malignant clones (lgl−/− RasV12) undergo caspase-mediated apoptosis and elimination.
source: Evidence that caspases are indeed activated in scrib−/− RasV12 clones is not only provided in this study, but also in a report that showed that small malignant clones (lgl−/− RasV12) undergo caspase-mediated apoptosis and elimination in a similar way as scrib clones (Menéndez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in this study and a citation to previous work.

claim: Only when mutant clones have reached a certain size, can they develop malignant tumors despite intrinsic caspase activation.
source: Only when mutant clones have reached a certain size, can they develop malignant tumors despite intrinsic caspase activation (Menéndez et al., 2010; Ballesteros-Arias et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: JNK activity acts both upstream and downstream of caspases and ROS generation in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones.
source: Our data suggest that JNK activity acts both upstream and downstream of caspases and ROS generation in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Initially, when the scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells form, a cell competition signal triggers JNK activation in scrib−/− RasV12 cells, similar to the events in scrib−/−-only mutant cells.
source: It is possible that initially, when the scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells form, a cell competition signal triggers JNK activation in scrib−/− RasV12 cells, similar to the events in scrib−/−-only mutant cells (Figure 6).
evidence: This is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: In both scrib−/− and scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells, JNK activity results in caspase activation.
source: In both scrib−/− and scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells, this JNK activity results in caspase activation (Figures 3 and 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 5A.

claim: Due to the anti-apoptotic activity of RasV12, caspases induce only very little apoptosis in scrib RasV12 clones.
source: However, due to the anti-apoptotic activity of RasV12, caspases induce only very little apoptosis in scrib RasV12 clones (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Although caspases are active, most scrib−/− RasV12 cells do not die and thus are in an 'undead'-like state.
source: Therefore, although caspases are active, most scrib−/− RasV12 cells do not die and thus are in an 'undead'-like state.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that caspases are active but most cells do not undergo apoptosis.

claim: Caspases promote the generation of extracellular ROS through activation of NADPH oxidase Duox in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
source: Caspases now promote the generation of extracellular ROS through activation of NADPH oxidase Duox.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Extracellular ROS recruit and activate hemocytes in scrib−/− RasV12 mosaic discs.
source: These ROS recruit and activate hemocytes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Hemocytes can release Eiger.
source: It is known that hemocytes can release Eiger (Cordero et al., 2010; Parisi et al., 2014; Fogarty et al., 2016) which signals through its receptor Grindelwald (Andersen et al., 2015) for further stimulation of JNK activity in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Eiger signals through its receptor Grindelwald for further stimulation of JNK activity in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
source: It is known that hemocytes can release Eiger (Cordero et al., 2010; Parisi et al., 2014; Fogarty et al., 2016) which signals through its receptor Grindelwald (Andersen et al., 2015) for further stimulation of JNK activity in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: JNK, caspases, ROS, hemocytes and Eiger constitute an amplification loop which may be necessary for tumor initiation.
source: Thus, we postulate that JNK, caspases, ROS, hemocytes and Eiger constitute an amplification loop (Figure 6) which may be necessary for tumor initiation.
evidence: This is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: Evidence of an amplification loop is provided by the mutual dependence of caspases, ROS and JNK.
source: Evidence of an amplification loop is provided by the mutual dependence of caspases, ROS and JNK (Figure 5; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar amplification loops have been described in apoptotic and 'undead' cells.
source: Similar amplification loops have been described in apoptotic and 'undead' cells (Wells et al., 2006; Shlevkov and Morata, 2012; Fogarty et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The amplification loop ensures persistent oncogenic signaling in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
source: This amplification loop ensures persistent oncogenic signaling in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the amplification loop maintains JNK and caspase activity.

claim: The amplification loop in scrib−/− RasV12 cells is in striking contrast to scrib−/− mutant cells alone in which JNK signaling triggers linear caspase activation and apoptosis.
source: This is in striking contrast to scrib−/− mutant cells alone in which JNK signaling triggers linear caspase activation and apoptosis (Brumby and Richardson, 2003; Igaki et al., 2006; Igaki et al., 2009; Uhlirova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In later stages of tumorigenesis, the amplification loop may have reached full strength and promotes malignant growth and invasion of scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
source: In later stages of tumorigenesis, the amplification loop may have reached full strength and promotes malignant growth and invasion of scrib−/− RasV12 cells (Figure 6).
evidence: This is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: Amplification loops have also been observed in other neoplastic tumor models in Drosophila.
source: Amplification loops have also been observed in other neoplastic tumor models in Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Intestinal stem cell tumors form in response to an amplification loop.
source: For example, intestinal stem cell tumors form in response to an amplification loop (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In a glycolytic tumor model, ROS are part of a amplification loop that facilitates metabolic reprogramming.
source: In a glycolytic tumor model, ROS are also part of a amplification loop that facilitates metabolic reprogramming (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It is possible that tumorigenesis in general depends on amplification loops to sustain oncogenic signaling.
source: Thus, it is possible that tumorigenesis in general depends on amplification loops to sustain oncogenic signaling.
evidence: This is speculative and based on inference from multiple examples.

claim: There are similarities and differences in the amplification loops of the 'undead' hyperplastic AiP model and the neoplastic scrib−/− RasV12 tumor model.
source: There are similarities and differences in the amplification loops of the 'undead' hyperplastic AiP model and the neoplastic scrib−/− RasV12 tumor model.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the two models.

claim: In both the 'undead' AiP model and the scrib−/− RasV12 model, caspases, ROS, hemocytes and JNK are required for growth.
source: In both models, caspases, ROS, hemocytes and JNK are required for growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The 'undead' AiP model only involves the initiator caspase Dronc for growth (effector caspases are inhibited by P35 in this model).
source: However, regarding caspases, the 'undead' AiP model only involves the initiator caspase Dronc for growth (in fact, effector caspases are inhibited by P35 in this model) (Fan et al., 2014; Huh et al., 2004; Pérez-Garijo et al., 2004; Pérez-Garijo et al., 2009; Ryoo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The neoplastic scrib−/− RasV12 model requires both initiator (Dronc) and effector (DrICE) caspases.
source: In contrast, the neoplastic scrib−/− RasV12 model requires both initiator (Dronc) and effector (DrICE) caspases.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of either Dronc or DrICE suppresses malignant growth and invasion in scrib−/− RasV12 clones.
source: Inhibition of either suppresses malignant growth and invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: While only extracellular ROS are essential in the 'undead' AiP model, neoplastic growth of scrib−/− RasV12 cells requires both intra- and extracellular ROS.
source: Another interesting difference is the differential involvement of ROS. While only extracellular ROS are essential in the 'undead' AiP model, neoplastic growth of scrib−/− RasV12 cells requires both intra- and extracellular ROS.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Mitochondria are the likely source of intracellular ROS because expression of mitochondrial SOD2 can suppress tumor growth and invasion of scrib−/− RasV12 tumors.
source: Mitochondria are the likely source of intracellular ROS because expression of mitochondrial SOD2 can suppress tumor growth and invasion of scrib−/− RasV12 tumors (Figure 1N).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that mitochondrial SOD2 suppresses tumor growth.

claim: It is unclear if the two populations of ROS (intra- and extracellular) are dependent or independent of each other.
source: It is unclear if these two populations of ROS are dependent or independent of each other.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: In endothelial cells, Nox-derived ROS can trigger an increase in mitochondrially-derived ROS and loss of mitochondrial membrane potential suggesting a dependence of mitochondrial ROS from Nox-generated ROS.
source: Recently, it was shown in endothelial cells that Nox-derived ROS can trigger an increase in mitochondrially-derived ROS and loss of mitochondrial membrane potential suggesting a dependence of mitochondrial ROS from Nox-generated ROS (Shafique et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It is possible that intra- and extracellular ROS are produced independently by caspase activity, and both are separately required for neoplastic transformation.
source: However, alternatively, it is also possible that intra- and extracellular ROS are produced independently by caspase activity, and both are separately required for neoplastic transformation.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: It is possible that 'genuine' AiP contributes to the tumor growth in scrib−/− RasV12.
source: Furthermore, while we mostly focused from the point-of-view of 'undead' AiP, it is also possible that 'genuine' AiP contributes to the tumor growth in scrib−/− RasV12.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: There are a few apoptotic cells in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones.
source: Consistent with this notion is the observation that there are a few apoptotic cells in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant clones (Figure 3E',F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E',F.

claim: Genuinely apoptotic cells can also produce ROS in Drosophila imaginal discs.
source: Genuinely apoptotic cells can also produce ROS in Drosophila imaginal discs (Santabárbara-Ruiz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Some of the differences between the 'undead' AiP model and the scrib−/− RasV12 model may be due to a combination of 'undead' and 'genuine' AiP in scrib−/− RasV12.
source: Therefore, it is tempting to speculate that some of the differences between the 'undead' AiP model and the scrib−/− RasV12 model are due to a combination of 'undead' and 'genuine' AiP in scrib−/− RasV12.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: The combination of 'undead' and 'genuine' AiP may explain the differences in caspase requirement, the differences in ROS production and the different outcomes of growth – hyperplastic vs. neoplastic – between the 'undead' AiP and the scrib−/− RasV12 tumor models.
source: This may explain the differences in caspase requirement, the differences in ROS production and the different outcomes of growth – hyperplastic vs. neoplastic – between the 'undead' AiP and the scrib−/− RasV12 tumor models.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: A known target of survival signaling by RasV12 is the pro-apoptotic gene Hid which acts upstream of caspase activation.
source: A known target of survival signaling by RasV12 is the pro-apoptotic gene Hid which acts upstream of caspase activation (Bergmann et al., 1998; Kurada and White, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Eiger and JNK can induce expression of hid.
source: Because Eiger and JNK can induce expression of hid (Moreno et al., 2002), it is possible that Hid activity is inhibited by oncogenic Ras.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It is possible that Hid activity is inhibited by oncogenic Ras.
source: Because Eiger and JNK can induce expression of hid (Moreno et al., 2002), it is possible that Hid activity is inhibited by oncogenic Ras.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: Inhibition of hid alone may not be sufficient to explain the altered caspase activity because inhibition of hid would result in loss of caspase activity.
source: However, while we do not exclude this possibility, it alone may not be sufficient to explain the altered caspase activity because inhibition of hid would result in loss of caspase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that caspases are still active in scrib−/− RasV12 cells.

claim: Caspases are still active in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells and they are able to induce apoptosis at least in a small amount of mutant cells.
source: However, caspases are still active in scrib−/− RasV12 mutant cells (Figure 3B,D) and they are also able to induce apoptosis at least in a small amount of mutant cells (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,D,E,F.

claim: It is possible that RasV12 modifies caspase activity in a different manner – directly or indirectly – for non-apoptotic ROS generation.
source: Therefore, it is possible that RasV12 modifies caspase activity in a different manner – directly or indirectly – for non-apoptotic ROS generation.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: Oncogenic Ras is mediating many steps in the tumorigenic process of scrib−/− RasV12 tissue.
source: Oncogenic Ras is mediating many steps in the tumorigenic process of scrib−/− RasV12 tissue.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: RasV12 changes the transcriptome of scrib−/− RasV12 cells and modifies the downstream activities of JNK.
source: It changes the transcriptome of these cells and modifies the downstream activities of JNK (Atkins et al., 2016; Külshammer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A critical step mediated by RasV12 is the modification of caspase activity – directly or indirectly – in the early stage of tumorigenesis in a way that the cells survive.
source: However, as shown in this work, a critical step mediated by RasV12 is the modification of caspase activity – directly or indirectly – in the early stage of tumorigenesis in a way that the cells survive.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: At present it is unclear if the caspase-modulating activity of RasV12 is dependent on transcription.
source: At present it is unclear if the caspase-modulating activity of RasV12 is dependent on transcription.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: There may not be enough time for a transcriptional response by the cell to escape the apoptotic activity of caspases.
source: There may not be enough time for a transcriptional response by the cell to escape the apoptotic activity of caspases.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: Work by others has suggested that changes in the transcriptome alone does not fully explain the neoplastic phenotype of scrib−/− RasV12 cells and that other potentially non-transcriptional processes are involved.
source: Consistently, work by others has suggested that changes in the transcriptome alone does not fully explain the neoplastic phenotype of scrib−/− RasV12 cells and that other potentially non-transcriptional processes are involved (Atkins et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Modification of caspase activity may be one of the non-transcriptional processes involved in the neoplastic phenotype of scrib−/− RasV12 cells.
source: Modification of caspase activity may be one of these non-transcriptional processes.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: Non-apoptotic functions of caspases have been reported.
source: Non-apoptotic functions of caspases have been reported (Shalini et al., 2015; Fogarty and Bergmann, 2017; Mukherjee and Williams, 2017; Nakajima and Kuranaga, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It is largely unknown how cells survive in the presence of activated caspases during non-apoptotic processes.
source: However, it is largely unknown how cells survive in the presence of activated caspases during non-apoptotic processes.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: It is possible that a reduction of caspase activity below a certain apoptotic threshold is sufficient for survival.
source: It is possible that a reduction of caspase activity below a certain apoptotic threshold is sufficient for survival.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: Other models for cell survival in the presence of activated caspases include changes in the subcellular localization of caspases or interaction with modifying factors such as Tango7.
source: Other models include changes in the subcellular localization of caspases or interaction with modifying factors such as Tango7 (D'Brot et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A recent study showed that mitochondrially-derived SCSβ restricts caspase activity for spermatid maturation in the Drosophila testis.
source: Interesting in this respect is a recent study which showed that mitochondrially-derived SCSβ restricts caspase activity for spermatid maturation in the Drosophila testis (Aram et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mitochondria release apoptotic signaling molecules such as cytochrome c and Smac during apoptosis.
source: Since mitochondria release apoptotic signaling molecules such as cytochrome c and Smac during apoptosis (Fuchs and Steller, 2011), it may also be possible that they release signals such as SCSβ or related factors which modulate the activity of caspases for non-apoptotic functions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.
